title: Imports and Dependencies
content: Imports $\texttt{Real.log}$ and $\texttt{Real.rpow}$ for logarithmic and real-power expressions in bounds, $\texttt{Finset.Card}$ for finite point configurations, and $\texttt{Tactic}$ for proof automation. The formalization works with $\texttt{Finset (\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R})}$ for finite planar point sets.
mathContext: The bounds involve $\log n$, $n^{-8/7}$, $n^{-7/6}$, requiring $\texttt{Real.log}$ and $\texttt{Real.rpow}$. Point sets are modeled as $\texttt{Finset (\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R})}$ with cardinality $n$.

title: Triangle Area via Determinant Formula
content: The signed area formula $\text{Area}(p,q,r) = \frac{1}{2}|x_1(y_2-y_3) + x_2(y_3-y_1) + x_3(y_1-y_2)|$ for three points in $\mathbb{R}^2$. This equals $\frac{1}{2}|\det \begin{pmatrix} x_1 - x_3 & x_2 - x_3 \\ y_1 - y_3 & y_2 - y_3 \end{pmatrix}|$, the absolute value of half the cross product of two edge vectors.
mathContext: $\text{Area}(p,q,r) = \frac{1}{2}|\vec{pq} \times \vec{pr}|$. Equivalently, twice the area equals $|\det(q-p, r-p)|$. This vanishes iff $p, q, r$ are collinear.

title: Unit Disk Point Configuration
content: A finite point set $P$ lies in the unit disk if $x^2 + y^2 \leq 1$ for every $(x,y) \in P$. The closed unit disk $\overline{\mathbb{D}} = \{(x,y) : x^2 + y^2 \leq 1\}$ is the standard domain for Heilbronn's problem. Using a disk (vs. unit square) is equivalent up to constants.
mathContext: $\texttt{IsInUnitDisk}(P) \iff \forall p \in P,\; p_1^2 + p_2^2 \leq 1$. The choice of convex domain (disk, square, triangle) affects constants but not the asymptotic exponent.

title: Minimum Triangle Area $\Delta_{\min}(P)$
content: The infimum of triangle areas over all distinct triples from a point set $P$: $\Delta_{\min}(P) = \inf_{p \neq q \neq r \in P} \text{Area}(p,q,r)$. Formalized using iterated $\inf$ ($\texttt{iInf}$) over membership and distinctness conditions. For finite sets, this infimum is attained.
mathContext: $\Delta_{\min}(P) = \min_{\{p,q,r\} \in \binom{P}{3}} \text{Area}(p,q,r)$. For $|P| = n$, there are $\binom{n}{3}$ triples to consider.

title: Heilbronn Function $\alpha(n)$
content: The Heilbronn function $\alpha(n) = \sup_{|P|=n,\, P \subset \overline{\mathbb{D}}} \Delta_{\min}(P)$: the supremum over all $n$-point configurations in the unit disk of the minimum triangle area. Equivalently, $\alpha(n)$ is the largest $\alpha$ such that every $n$-point set in $\overline{\mathbb{D}}$ contains a triangle of area $\leq \alpha$. The problem: estimate $\alpha(n)$ as $n \to \infty$.

title: Erdős's Lower Bound $\alpha(n) \gg 1/n^2$
content: Erdős observed that a greedy placement achieves $\alpha(n) \geq c/n^2$: place points sequentially, and at each step the forbidden region (where a new point would create a triangle of area $< c/n^2$) has measure $O(n^2 \cdot c/n^2 \cdot 1/n) = O(c/n) < 1$ for small $c$. This was the starting point for the lower bound side.
mathContext: $\alpha(n) \geq c/n^2$ for some absolute $c > 0$. The greedy argument: each existing pair $(p_i, p_j)$ forbids a strip of width $O(\alpha/\|p_i - p_j\|)$ for the next point.

title: Trivial Upper Bound $\alpha(n) \ll 1/n$
content: The pigeonhole principle gives $\alpha(n) \leq C/n$: divide the unit disk into $\lfloor n/3 \rfloor$ parallel strips of width $O(1/n)$; by pigeonhole, some strip contains $\geq 3$ points, forming a triangle of area $\leq O(1/n)$. This was the first upper bound, predating all sophisticated methods.
mathContext: $\alpha(n) \leq C/n$. Partition into $n/3$ strips of width $O(1/n)$; three points in one strip form a triangle of height $\leq O(1/n)$ and base $\leq 2$.

title: KPS Lower Bound $\alpha(n) \gg (\log n)/n^2$
content: Komlós, Pintz, and Szemerédi (1982) improved Erdős's lower bound by a logarithmic factor: $\alpha(n) \geq c(\log n)/n^2$. Their probabilistic argument uses a random point placement with a more careful analysis of the forbidden region, showing that the greedy construction can be refined via the Lovász Local Lemma. This remains the best known lower bound after 40+ years.
mathContext: $\alpha(n) \geq c \cdot \frac{\log n}{n^2}$ [KPS82]. Key idea: random placement in a grid-like structure; the local lemma handles dependent forbidden events. Gap from trivial: multiplicative $\log n$ improvement.

title: KPS Upper Bound $\alpha(n) \ll n^{-8/7}$
content: Komlós, Pintz, and Szemerédi (1981) proved $\alpha(n) \leq C/n^{8/7}$, the first improvement over the trivial $1/n$ bound. Their proof uses the Szemerédi regularity lemma to find structure in point configurations: any $n$-point set must contain a dense bipartite-like substructure that forces many small triangles. The exponent $8/7 \approx 1.143$ stood as the best upper bound for over 40 years.
mathContext: $\alpha(n) \leq C \cdot n^{-8/7}$ [KPS81]. Regularity lemma decomposes the point set into clusters; between regular pairs, the point distribution forces small triangles. Exponent improved from $1$ to $8/7$.

title: Cohen–Pohoata–Zakharov Upper Bound $\alpha(n) \ll n^{-7/6-o(1)}$
content: Cohen, Pohoata, and Zakharov (2024) achieved the current best upper bound $\alpha(n) \leq C/n^{7/6+o(1)}$, improving the KPS exponent from $8/7 \approx 1.143$ to $7/6 \approx 1.167$. Their breakthrough uses incidence geometry techniques—specifically point-line and point-curve incidence bounds—combined with the polynomial method. The $o(1)$ term in the exponent comes from a logarithmic correction.
mathContext: $\alpha(n) \leq C \cdot n^{-7/6+o(1)}$ [CPZ24]. Improvement: $8/7 = 1.\overline{142857} \to 7/6 = 1.1\overline{6}$. Uses Szemerédi–Trotter type incidence bounds and the polynomial partitioning method of Guth–Katz.
